presentingComplaint: Progressive leg swelling, frothy urine, and increasing fatigue over the past 3 months in a man with long-standing type 2 diabetes.
history: 61-year-old man with a 15-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus (last HbA1c 8.9%) and hypertension for 10 years, on metformin, glimepiride, and amlodipine. He reports progressive bilateral ankle and pretibial swelling over 3 months, frothy discoloration of urine noticed by his wife, reduced appetite, nausea, and generalized fatigue. No dysuria, no gross hematuria, no fevers. He has known diabetic retinopathy (laser-treated 4 years ago) and mild sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy. No NSAID use, no recent contrast exposure. No prior known kidney disease diagnosis but has missed several outpatient follow-ups over the past 2 years. Family history negative for polycystic kidney disease.
examination: Alert, mildly puffy-faced, oriented. Bilateral pitting pedal and pretibial edema to mid-shin. No rash, no oral ulcers. Chest clear, no crackles. JVP mildly raised. Cardiac exam: no murmur, regular rhythm. Abdomen soft, non-tender, no ascites clinically. Fundoscopy: background diabetic retinopathy with laser scars. Reduced vibration sense and ankle reflexes bilaterally consistent with diabetic peripheral neuropathy. No asterixis. No pericardial rub.

differentialDiagnoses: Diabetic nephropathy (diabetic kidney disease) with CKD stage 4
Primary glomerulonephritis (e.g., membranous nephropathy, FSGS) superimposed on diabetes
Contrast- or NSAID-induced acute-on-chronic kidney injury (no exposure history)
finalDiagnosis: Diabetic nephropathy (diabetic kidney disease) causing CKD stage 4 (eGFR 15-29 mL/min/1.73m2)

contraindications: Avoid nephrotoxic agents (NSAIDs, IV contrast without precaution, aminoglycosides)
Metformin should be discontinued/dose-reconsidered at eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73m2 per label and KDIGO guidance
Caution with RAAS inhibitor initiation given baseline hyperkalemia (K 5.3) - correct potassium and monitor closely before/after starting ACEi/ARB
SGLT2 inhibitors generally not initiated de novo at eGFR <20 mL/min/1.73m2 (formulation-dependent; check product-specific eGFR cutoff)
edgeCases: Absence of diabetic retinopathy would raise suspicion for a non-diabetic glomerular disease and should prompt consideration of renal biopsy
Active urinary sediment (dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts) would argue against pure diabetic nephropathy and favor glomerulonephritis, warranting biopsy
Rapid decline in eGFR (over weeks) is atypical for diabetic nephropathy and should trigger evaluation for a superimposed acute process

Renal biopsy is not routinely required when the clinical picture (long-standing diabetes, retinopathy, proteinuria, bland sediment, gradual course) is classic for diabetic nephropathy
